title: Testing the Rules as Executed against the Rules as Promised

authors.name: Anne Schuth

abstract: Where government executes the law from formalized rules, the formalization has to be tested against what the statute was meant to yield. But the expected outcomes a test needs almost always come from the formalizer, so the tests inherit the reading they were meant to check. The Dutch legislative record holds an oracle that neither the encoder nor the executing organization sets: the worked examples with which the government shows parliament what a bill should arrive at. A full-text harvest scores 5,068 passages in 2,415 documents as candidates, and a recall check suggests the harvest finds at most about half. We transcribed seventeen examples under a rule that forbids inventing cases and ran fifteen against a public corpus of encoded statutes. The other two exemplify provisions the corpus does not model. Eleven reproduce the promised amount. Among the four failures is a household the government’s own amendment note had falsified before the act took effect, and auditing the expectations around it found three defects in our encodings. The same material shows what the oracle cannot do. An example states a third of the inputs an encoding needs, and rarely places one on a threshold. Of the 53 faults seeded into the allowance scheme, the encoders’ twelve scenarios catch 23 and two built from the memorandum’s arithmetic catch 12, each missing what the other finds. Examples go stale as soon as a parameter moves, and they rarely touch the open norms where the concretizations live. Worked examples belong in the record of how a statute becomes executable rules: the specification file the Council of State asked for in 2021, maintained with the law and layered with the policy rules and judgments that carry what a memorandum cannot.
